name: Alar batten graft

lead: An alar batten graft is a small piece of cartilage, usually taken from the patient's own septum, ear or rib, placed along the side wall of the nostril to hold it open. It treats nasal valve collapse, where the nostril wall caves inward on breathing in, often after earlier rhinoplasty, trauma or ageing.

For appearance, a supported sidewall can prevent pinched, collapsed nostrils and keep a natural-looking nostril rim, which is why it appears in hard-maxxing discussions of rhinoplasty. Studies report notable breathing improvement and also evaluate aesthetic outcomes.

paras: A surgeon places the graft through an incision in or around the nose as part of functional rhinoplasty, often alongside other grafts or septoplasty. It is performed under anaesthesia, with recovery like other nasal surgery.

Risks are those of rhinoplasty: swelling that can take a year or more to settle, possible revision (roughly 5 to 20% of rhinoplasties), and graft-related issues such as visibility or irregularity. Implants such as porous polyethylene have been reported to extrude in the internal valve in case reports.

chain: Cartilage strip placed in the nostril wall
Open, stable nostril shape and clearer breathing
angle.text: The graft braces a weak sidewall so the nostril keeps its shape. It is mainly functional but also used to support the nostril contour during or after rhinoplasty.

lead: An alar batten graft is a cartilage graft placed along the underside or sidewall of the lower lateral cartilage to support a collapsing nostril wall. It is one of several cartilage-grafting techniques for the internal nasal valve, alongside spreader, butterfly, autospreader and alar composite grafts.[1]

Nasal valve collapse has a lifetime prevalence of up to 13% and can follow prior rhinoplasty, other procedures, facial paralysis, congenital defects, trauma or ageing; it impairs nasal breathing.[1] Surgeons weigh function, cosmesis and technical difficulty when choosing among approaches.[1]
In the looksmaxxing community the graft appears within discussions of rhinoplasty and the nose. Its look-related role is to maintain a stable, well-shaped nostril wall while restoring breathing.
infobox: Internal and external nasal valve collapse

paras: Techniques for the internal nasal valve fall into cartilage grafting, implants and suture suspension. Cartilage grafts include the alar batten, butterfly, spreader, autospreader and alar composite grafts.[1] Grafts usually come from the septum, and surgeons may use ear or rib cartilage when septal supply is insufficient, as in revision surgery.[2]
A sub-alar variant places the graft under the lateral crus of the lower lateral cartilage.[3] A transoral approach has also been described for orthognathic jaw surgery patients.[4]

A prospective study of 126 patients with nasal valve collapse treated with autologous alar batten grafts reported that 94% at 6 months and 97% at 1 year reported improvement, and examined nasal steroid use and allergic symptoms.[5]

A 2009 study of 80 patients (54 female, 26 male) treated with alar batten grafts evaluated functional and aesthetic results across iatrogenic and posttraumatic groups.[6] A study of sub-alar battens evaluated functional results in 27 patients.[3]

A 2025 systematic review of 15 studies (1,052 patients; 362 alar batten, 690 lateral crural strut) found NOSE score improvements of 25.6 to 69.0 points for alar batten graft studies and 15.8 to 65.6 for lateral crural strut studies, presented as ranges because of heterogeneous designs.[7]

Rhinoplasty outcomes can be unpredictable, swelling may take a year or more to resolve and smoking impairs healing; revision is needed in roughly 5 to 20% of cases.[2] Case reports describe extrusion of porous polyethylene implants in the internal nasal valve.[8]
